entries.headline: Pennsylvania's countdown narrows to a single working day before the October 13 deadline, with Rep. Doyle Heffley planning a floor amendment for a six month delay and Rep. Russ Diamond and House Democratic leadership publicly trading blame over which chamber must move first. A sponsor question on House Bill 2793 gets resolved. Oklahoma, Iowa and the rest of the priority states stayed quiet, and the week's only primary change in the legislative feed turned out to be a stale metadata refresh on an already known bill.

items.text: The legislative feed refreshed again, generated at 16:08 UTC on October 6, 2026, one day after the prior scan reported here. Totals moved to 308 matching bills, 85 primary and 223 secondary, with two changed records and none new. The primary changed record is Pennsylvania House Bill 2213, the flat fee House companion to Senate Bill 1079 already reported on this page, and its own last action date of February 11, 2026 did not move, so this again looks like a metadata refresh rather than new committee or floor action. The secondary changed record, New Jersey Senate Bill 4227, prohibits fur farming and matched only on the phrase amusement device in passing, so it is not reported further.

With six days left to the October 13 deadline, the House and Senate had only one scheduled session day left to act before then, today, October 7, with the next session day not until October 19, six days after the stay is due to expire. Reporting on October 6 said Rep. Doyle Heffley plans to offer a floor amendment that would delay enforcement by six months, and quoted him urging leadership to let the chamber vote: 'We've seen Democrats here. We've seen Republicans here. This is bipartisan.' No committee vote or floor vote had been confirmed as of this search.

Rep. Russ Diamond publicly pressed House leadership on October 5 not to let the deadline pass without a vote, saying Senate Republican leadership's insistence that any skill games bill originate in the Senate stands in the way of action, and offering to add public transportation funding to his own two bills to attract Democratic votes. A spokesperson for House Majority Leader Matt Bradford countered that Senate Republicans had demanded control of the issue but failed to pass their own measure, and said House Democrats remain willing to reach a resolution that also ensures a safe and equitable framework. Neither side described a specific vote count or timeline.

A clarification on a bill this page could not previously attribute. Pennsylvania Petroleum Association reporting from September 27 identifies House Bill 2793 as Rep. Manuel Guzman's extension bill, temporarily authorizing skill games through April 13, 2027, running parallel to Rep. Brad Roae's House Bill 2795, which carries the same expiration date. Both were referred to the House Gaming Oversight Committee on September 24 and neither has been scheduled for a vote.

entries.headline: Week in review: Pennsylvania's standoff hardened this week with about a dozen competing bills in play and no vote in sight, Oklahoma's sweepstakes platforms kept thinning out ahead of November 1, and a Washington tribal compact became the first new federal gaming notice since mid July. This is the longest unbroken stretch without a single change across 304 tracked bills nationwide since this watch began, and it remains worth a manual check of the workflow's run history in the skill-games-watch repository rather than continuing to treat the silence as confirmed quiet.

The General Assembly remained deadlocked this week with roughly a dozen competing bills in play and no committee vote or floor schedule set for any of them. Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman said he was not optimistic a deal could pass before the deadline, and House Democrats called on Senate Republicans to show they can pass something. Senate Democrat Marty Flynn said he may end up supporting legislation he does not fully endorse just to reach a solution, and put the annual taxable revenue at stake at roughly a billion dollars. No tax or extension proposal, including House Bills 2801, 2802, 1050 and 2213, Senate Bill 1079, or the Roae and Guzman extension memos, has advanced out of committee. Eleven days remain to the October 13 deadline.

Sweepstakes platforms kept narrowing Oklahoma access ahead of the November 1 effective date. Pulsz and Pulsz Bingo restricted Oklahoma players to Gold Coin only play, and Lucky Rush added the state to its fully restricted list, extending the pattern of exits that began with AceBet and Cluck in August. No enforcement guidance from the attorney general or state gaming authorities and no legal challenge to the statute have been found in searches this week. Thirty days remain to the effective date.

Rep. Russ Diamond's previously announced two bill package now carries bill numbers. House Bill 2801 and House Bill 2802, reported September 24, would regulate skill games at a 20 percent tax rate, cap locations at five machines for clubs, liquor licensed restaurants, bars and qualified truck stops, cut the casino slot tax rate to 49.9 percent, and route the new revenue to annual dividend payments for Pennsylvania's roughly 2.87 million qualified homeowners. Neither bill has been scheduled for a committee vote.

A coalition called PlayPA for Charity, including the American Legion and the VFW, is pressing lawmakers to pass House Bill 1050, which would legalize electronic pull tab machines for charitable gaming, raise the single prize limit from 2,000 to 5,000 dollars, raise the weekly per club prize cap from 35,000 to 70,000 dollars, and lower the required public interest payout from 60 to 25 percent. Reported September 28 and 29, the push is separate from the skill games tax bills but reflects the same pressure on veterans posts and fraternal clubs as the October 13 deadline approaches.

Attorney General Dave Sunday said publicly on September 29 that his office will act in accordance with the law once the stay expires, echoing and reinforcing the State Police guidance already reported here: seizures, forfeiture and criminal charges for businesses and distributors that have not removed machines by October 14, and unplugging a machine is not compliance. He said a slot machine does not stop being a slot machine because it has been turned off. No tax or extension bill has passed either chamber, and thirteen days remain to the deadline.

No new enforcement guidance from the attorney general or state gaming authorities, no legal challenge to the statute, and no additional operator exit beyond the AceBet and Cluck restrictions already reported turned up in searches this week. Thirty two days remain to the November 1 effective date.

Still no first cease and desist order against a dual currency sweepstakes operator has been published since the Racing and Gaming Commission's authority took effect July 1. Nothing new found this week.

The Federal Register's Indian Affairs Bureau index was reachable directly this run rather than through a blocked search, and it lists no Indian Gaming compact notice or Class III compact approval published in September 2026. The most recent gaming related entry remains the Wyandotte Nation and Kansas compact approved by operation of law on July 14.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton issued Opinion KP-0520 on June 11, 2026, concluding that a device violates the Penal Code's gambling definition so long as chance plays any role in whether the player obtains something of value, regardless of whether the operator markets it as a skill game. The opinion was requested by a district attorney over slot-style machines paired with a memory game such as Follow Me, and it gives prosecutors and law enforcement statewide grounds to treat those machines as illegal gambling devices rather than exempt amusement. This predates this watch's baseline of September 19 and was not previously reported here; it surfaced through this run's search rather than the legislative feed. It sits in tension with a 2024 Van Zandt County district court ruling and a split 2025 appellate decision that found a similar memory-game machine to be skill based, so enforcement in practice still appears to vary by county, and no prosecution citing the opinion directly has been found yet.

The legislature reconvenes Monday, September 28, with about six scheduled session days left before the October 13 stay expires, Senate co-sponsor Gene Yaw told WITF this week. This is the fourth consecutive run drawing on that same file. If the underlying GitHub Actions workflow has stalled, bill activity anywhere in the country could be going unreported, and it is worth a manual check of the workflow's run history.

No movement was found this week on the other standing fronts. The North Carolina Supreme Court has not ruled in No Limit Games v. Sheriff of Robeson County following the September 9 argument. Florida's suit against VGW, Stake and their payment processors shows no new docket activity since it was filed in Hillsborough County Circuit Court in August. Iowa's Racing and Gaming Commission has not published a first cease-and-desist order under SF 2289. No Indian Gaming compact notice newer than the Wyandotte Nation and Kansas compact of July 14 has appeared in the Federal Register. Targeted searches for Virginia, Missouri, Georgia, South Carolina, Texas, Ohio, Maryland, Mississippi, New York, New Jersey, California, Connecticut, Montana, Louisiana, Michigan, Washington, Illinois, Nevada and Wisconsin, and for Pace-O-Matic, Torch Electronics and Great Lakes Amusement specifically, turned up nothing new in the last seven days.

No revival of the risk-free redesign or new challenge to the gray machines ban was found. A same-numbered HB 594 exists in the 2026 regular session, but it concerns sex offender restrictions on Halloween activities and has nothing to do with gaming machines, so this is not the vehicle that upheld the ban in 2024. Nothing else on the underlying litigation turned up this week.

No change to the 20 percent of net tax, the four machine per location limit, the 3 dollar maximum wager or the 3,000 dollar payout cap was found, and no news of a lab certification change. The only recent related item is a Casper city council gambling expansion moratorium from April 2026 that the coverage says leaves skill-based games untouched, which is local zoning rather than a change to the state framework.

entries.headline: VGW retires LuckyLand Slots nationwide and Pennsylvania's flat-fee bills get numbers for the first time, while Oklahoma, Iowa and federal tribal compact activity stay quiet three weeks before Pennsylvania's stay expires.

items.text: Local coverage on 17 and 18 September attached bill numbers, for the first time in this watch, to two previously described flat-fee proposals: Senate Bill 1079 from Sen. Gene Yaw and House Bill 2213 from Rep. Danilo Burgos, both setting a 500 dollar per machine per month fee and capping the statewide total at 50,000 machines. Neither has been scheduled for a vote. The same coverage describes the Pennsylvania State Police plan for 14 October as encouraging voluntary compliance rather than immediate seizure, which reads softer than the department's own 9 September guidance that machines become subject to seizure and forfeiture that day. The discrepancy is unresolved and is worth confirming directly with PSP.
No new enforcement guidance, operator exit announcement or legal challenge to the Sweeps Coin ban turned up this week. The effective date is six weeks away on 1 November.
No first cease-and-desist order against a dual-currency sweepstakes operator has been reported since the Racing and Gaming Commission's authority took effect on 1 July.

VGW Holdings completed the shutdown of its LuckyLand Slots sweepstakes brand on 14 September 2026, ending nearly eight years of operation. The wind-down began 29 July, with Gold Coin sales stopping 3 August and gameplay halting 24 August, following founder Laurence Escalante's resignation in July amid criminal charges and a broader retreat of VGW's larger Chumba brand from sixteen states. The closure changes no law but continues the pattern of operator exits and pressure that has followed New York's settlement with VGW and Florida's suit against it.

The legislative feed's most current file is still the one generated at 15:50 UTC on 19 September 2026, showing zero new or changed bills against the same totals as the last run: 304 matching, 82 primary and 222 secondary. No fresher LegiScan data was available as of this run on 21 September, so no state's bill activity could be checked beyond what was already reported.

A direct search of the Federal Register's own search tool was again blocked to automated access, so this check relied on indexed web search. No Indian Gaming compact notice newer than the Wyandotte Nation and Kansas compact published 14 July 2026 was found; the nearest items located, an Upper Skagit Indian Tribe and Washington compact notice and a Class III compact process notice, both predate 14 July. Treat this as not found rather than confirmed absent.

entries.headline: Pennsylvania State Police tell businesses to physically remove skill games before 13 October, and say unplugging them is not compliance.

items.text: The Pennsylvania State Police issued compliance guidance on 9 September 2026 ahead of the stay expiring. It tells establishments to remove skill game machines now and states that simply powering off an otherwise operable machine or unplugging it is not sufficient to comply with the law. From 14 October, PSP says machines, associated equipment and the money associated with their operation are subject to seizure and forfeiture, and criminal charges may follow. The release directs establishments to contact their distributor or vendor to arrange removal, and says that if a vendor refuses, the establishment is encouraged to contact PSP for help removing the machines.

Rep. Brad Roae of Crawford and Erie counties filed a co-sponsorship memo on Monday 14 September 2026 for legislation that would push the enforcement deadline from 13 October 2026 to 13 April 2027, temporarily legalizing the machines without taxing them while a permanent framework is negotiated. No bill number has appeared and the legislative feed shows no new Pennsylvania bill introduced as of 19 September, so this remains a memo rather than filed legislation.

Rep. Russ Diamond announced a two bill package on 2 September 2026 that puts detail behind his 20 percent number, and the detail matters more than the rate for anyone placing machines. It would cap locations at five machines, limit eligibility to clubs, bars and restaurants holding liquor licenses plus qualified truck stops, and exclude convenience stores, gas stations and dedicated skill game parlors. It would also cut the casino slot rate to 49.9 percent and route revenue to property tax relief. Diamond said on 9 September the bills were likely to be introduced within the week; they have not appeared in the feed.

No tax proposal has passed either chamber. The House and Senate each have about six voting days scheduled between 28 September and 7 October, which is the whole runway before the stay expires. Two figures in circulation conflict and are worth pinning down before anyone relies on them: the Senate Republican rate is reported as 35 percent in some coverage and 36 percent in other coverage, and the installed base is given as roughly 70,000 devices in court and law enforcement coverage against an industry estimate of about 50,000 machines.

County prosecutors are positioning for the handover. The Bucks County District Attorney's office said on 18 September 2026 that it will consult with the State Police but that troopers are leading enforcement, with the county prosecuting cases referred to it. No grace period beyond 13 October has been described by any Pennsylvania agency so far.

Attorney General Letitia James announced on 9 September 2026 that VGW Holdings, which runs Chumba Casino, Global Poker and LuckyLand Slots, will pay 8 million dollars in disgorgement, penalties and costs and must stop offering sweeps coin play in New York. The office alleged that coins presented as free were in practice obtained at roughly one coin per dollar spent, which is the same characterization other attorneys general have used against the dual currency model.

The North Carolina Supreme Court heard argument on 9 September 2026 in No Limit Games v. Sheriff of Robeson County, on whether video sweepstakes terminals fall foul of the state ban where chance determines the prize even if the game itself is skill based. The Court of Appeals ruled against the operator two to one in December 2024. No decision has issued and one could land at any time. One outlet dated the argument 11 September, which is a Friday and inconsistent with the court's sitting, so 9 September is the date carried here.

Carried forward because it was not on this page and it bears directly on sweepstakes exposure. Attorney General James Uthmeier sued VGW and the Stake entities in Hillsborough County Circuit Court on 19 August 2026, and named their payment processors as defendants alongside them, including Trustly, Worldpay, Yodlee, Praxis and Breeze Labs. Some coverage dates the filing 20 August. The theory reaches the payment layer the same way Oklahoma's statute does, and no docket movement was reported in the past week.

Nothing found this week. No enforcement guidance, no legal challenge and no newly announced operator exit ahead of the 1 November effective date turned up in searches. Six weeks out, the absence of any published enforcement posture from the attorney general or state gaming authorities is itself the notable fact, since liability under the statute reaches payment processors, geolocation providers, suppliers, platform providers and media affiliates rather than operators alone.

Still no first enforcement action. The Racing and Gaming Commission's only September posting is the August revenue report dated 16 September 2026, and no cease and desist order against a dual currency operator has been published since the authority took effect on 1 July.

The legislative feed generated at 15:50 UTC on 19 September 2026 returned zero new bills, zero changed bills and zero that stopped matching, against unchanged totals of 304 matching, 82 primary and 222 secondary. Nothing to report from any state, and the empty result is a useful cross check on the Pennsylvania items above, since neither the Roae nor the Diamond proposal has been formally introduced.

Federal activity could not be checked as thoroughly as the rest. The Federal Register query needed an approval that no one was present to give in an unattended run, so the check fell back to a domain restricted search, which surfaced no Indian Gaming notice published after the Wyandotte Nation and Kansas compact on 14 July 2026. Treat this as not found rather than confirmed absent, and it is worth a manual look.

entries.headline: Baseline established. Two hard deadlines inside seven weeks, and two states moved off the quiet list.

items.text: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court held on 15 June 2026 that skill games are slot machines under the Gaming Act and Crimes Code, and stayed enforcement for 120 days to let the legislature act. Five tax proposals are competing: 52 percent from the Shapiro administration, 35 percent from Senate Republicans, 20 percent from Rep. Russ Diamond, 16 percent from Sen. Yaw, and a flat 500 dollars per unit per month from Sens. Yaw and Williams. No proposal had passed as of this entry.

Governor Stitt vetoed the dual-currency sweepstakes ban on 7 May 2026 and the legislature overrode him on 15 May, Senate 34 to 10 and House 68 to 19. The ban takes effect 1 November 2026. Liability reaches past the operator to payment processors, geolocation providers, gaming suppliers, platform providers and media affiliates. Tribal gaming under IGRA and charitable gaming are exempt. Operators are lawfully live until the effective date.

Signed by Governor Reynolds and effective 1 July 2026, giving the Iowa Racing and Gaming Commission authority to issue cease-and-desist orders against unlicensed operators, reaching dual-currency sweepstakes products. High 5 Casino and Baba Casino exited before the effective date; Stake.us, WOW Vegas and Chumba Casino did not. No enforcement action has been reported since, which is the thing to watch.

Legislative baseline seeded from LegiScan across all 50 states: 304 bills match the keyword set for the current sessions, of which 82 carry the subject in the bill title or description and 222 mention it only in the full text. Subsequent runs report only what is new or what changed.
